title: Knowledge Check 7: Lessons 49-56
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 49-56 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why can a web application firewall not serve as a complete semantic safety layer for an AI application?
options: It inspects only the response body and never the incoming request at all
It cannot be deployed in front of a model endpoint
It matches text patterns, not meaning, so rephrased attacks slip past it
It already enforces the authentication the gateway provides
questions.explanation: A firewall reads surface text, not meaning, so paraphrased or encoded injections evade its rules. Catching those requires a separate control that interprets the prompt.

questions.question: Why must data loss prevention watch what an agent sends through outputs and tool calls, not only what a user types?
options: Sensitive data also leaves through responses and tool calls
User input is never sensitive enough to require any inspection
Tool calls travel outside the network and bypass every control
Outputs are encrypted, so they need separate decryption first
questions.explanation: Sensitive content can leave through what the model returns or what a tool call forwards, so guarding only the request side leaves the other half of the flow open. The control must cover the full data path.

questions.question: Which set of controls belongs at the API gateway rather than at the network edge?
options: Volumetric rate limiting and strict request size limits
Authentication, authorization, and per-tenant quotas
GPU scheduling and model placement
Embedding storage and vector search
questions.explanation: The gateway is the single choke point where identity is verified and per-identity policy is applied. Volume controls like rate and size limits belong earlier, at the edge.

questions.question: Why is a customer ID on its own still treated as personal data in an agent pipeline?
options: Because any identifier that can point to a person counts as personal data
Because customer IDs always contain a name embedded somewhere in the string
Because only data that names a person explicitly is considered regulated
Because IDs are treated as personal data only once they are stored
questions.explanation: Personal data covers anything that can identify a person directly or in combination with other information, so recognition must span the assembled context rather than only obvious fields like a name.

questions.question: Where does data minimization have to live for it to actually work?
options: In a system prompt that asks the model to use only necessary data
In a review meeting held after the agent has already shipped
In the architecture, in what the pipeline fetches and passes
In the model's training data, which filters out excess fields
questions.explanation: A prompt instruction is a request the model may ignore, so over-collection happens before the model is even called. Minimization is a control you build into retrieval, the tool interface, and input transformation.

questions.question: Why does retention for an agent have to be applied per store rather than once?
options: Because each store has a different legal jurisdiction
Because the data becomes many separate copies of the same record
Because databases cannot run scheduled deletions
Because the model refuses to delete any of its own cached context
questions.explanation: The prompt, retrieved context, trace, embeddings, and logs are each separate copies of the same personal data. Removing only the source record leaves the person's data retained elsewhere, so each store needs its own expiration.

questions.question: An agent must act on behalf of a specific user, with that user's approval, without ever seeing the password. Which flow fits?
options: The client credentials grant, because the agent acts with its own identity
The authorization code grant, because the user approves the access
A shared human account, because it already has the user's permissions
A long-lived static API key stored in the agent's configuration
questions.explanation: Delegated work uses the authorization code grant: the user authenticates and approves at the authorization server, and the password never reaches the agent. The client credentials grant is for an agent acting on its own behalf with no user in the loop.

questions.question: Why give a long-running agent its own service account instead of borrowing a human's credentials?
options: A service account is a non-human identity with its own credentials
A service account inherits the full permissions of whoever created it
A service account never needs its credentials rotated or stored securely
A service account lets the agent skip authentication to the resource server
questions.explanation: A service account is a separate principal with its own credentials and permissions, so the agent does not borrow a human's access or share a human's secret. It can be scoped, rotated, and revoked without touching any person.

questions.question: What limits the damage if an agent's token or key leaks?
options: The model's system prompt, which tells it to refuse harmful calls
The provider, which detects and blocks unauthorized requests
The scopes granted to the token, which the server enforces
The agent's logs, which record what the attacker does
questions.explanation: Scopes express least privilege: the token can do only what it was granted, and the resource server enforces that on each request. The narrower the scope, the smaller the blast radius when credentials leak.

questions.question: A prompt tries to make the agent read another tenant's records. What actually keeps the boundary?
options: The system prompt telling the model to stay within the current tenant
Row-level security and the tenant filter on retrieval
The model's refusal to follow instructions naming another tenant
A content filter that flags the request as suspicious
questions.explanation: Isolation is a programmatic guarantee in the data plane, not a prompt instruction. The database and the retrieval filter refuse anything outside the session tenant, so the model never has a chance to cross the boundary.

questions.question: Why is counting requests an inadequate quota for a multi-tenant agent?
options: One agent turn can consume thousands of tokens in a single call
Request counts are always higher than the provider actually allows
Agents use tool calls instead of requests, so the count stays at zero
Rate limits are shared and cannot be configured per tenant
questions.explanation: For an LLM the unit of consumption is the token, not the request. A single turn can burn thousands of tokens or a stalled loop can drain a day's budget across few requests, so the quota must count tokens and cost.

questions.question: Isolation and abuse prevention are different controls. What does isolation alone fail to stop?
options: A tenant reading its own records
A database that enforces row-level security
A vector store that filters retrieval by tenant
A tenant exhausting the shared model budget
questions.explanation: Isolation stops data crossing the tenant boundary, but it does nothing about one tenant consuming the shared budget. That is a capacity problem, which quotas and abuse detection address.

questions.question: Which failure should not be retried because retrying it only delays a fix?
options: A rate-limited response that will clear
A temporary service-unavailable response
An unauthorized response from bad credentials
A gateway timeout from an overloaded upstream
questions.explanation: An unauthorized response is a permanent failure on your side, like a malformed request or a wrong endpoint. Retrying it wastes time and hides the real configuration bug; only transient server-side failures are worth retrying.

questions.question: Why add jitter on top of exponential backoff?
options: Jitter removes the delay so retries happen immediately
Clients that fail together would retry in a synchronized spike
Jitter converts a transient failure into a permanent failure instead
Jitter guarantees the server's retry hint is always respected
questions.explanation: Backoff alone makes every client that failed at the same instant wait the same amount and retry together, re-creating the overload. Jitter randomizes the waits so the retries spread out across the window.

questions.question: What does an open circuit breaker change about a request to a provider that is down?
options: The request is rejected fast instead of waiting on a timeout
The request is buffered until the provider recovers
The request is retried more aggressively until it finally succeeds
The request is routed to a faster model automatically
questions.explanation: When the breaker is open, requests fail immediately or skip to the fallback instead of each burning a full timeout. That fast rejection is what separates a clean failover from a cascading slowdown.

questions.question: Which latency number matters most for a human who reads an answer as it arrives?
options: End-to-end latency, because it measures the whole response
Time to first token, because the reader stops waiting
Time per output token, because faster tokens read better
Batch size, because it sets how responsive the reply feels
questions.explanation: Once the stream outpaces reading speed, the only wait a person consciously feels is the silence before the first token. For a human reader, time to first token is the experience.

questions.question: When the consumer of a model call is another system that blocks on the full completion, what is the right move?
options: Stream the response so the machine sees tokens sooner
Lower the per-token rate as far as possible
Turn streaming off and optimize the full completion
Add batching to the single request to speed it up
questions.explanation: A downstream service cannot act on partial output, so streaming just moves the same wait around without hiding it. For a machine consumer, the binding number is end-to-end latency.

questions.question: Why does continuous batching outperform static batching?
options: It admits and evicts work at each decode step to keep the GPU busy
It runs each request on a separate GPU with no sharing
It removes the need for any latency budget at all
It keeps every request in a single batch until all of them have finished
questions.explanation: Static batching holds a whole set together until its slowest member finishes, wasting time as output lengths vary. Continuous batching fills freed slots at every decode step, keeping the GPU busy and freeing short requests early.

questions.question: Why must an agent worker be stateless for horizontal scaling to help?
options: Because a worker can only call a model provider when it is stateless
Because context held in one worker's memory ties it there
Because stateless workers use no memory while they run
Because state is never allowed in any distributed system
questions.explanation: If each request's context is held in a worker's memory, that worker is the only one that can finish it, so extra copies cannot help. The state has to live somewhere any worker can reach.

questions.question: Which queue measurement is the honest signal for when to add workers?
options: A steady empty queue with idle workers
A high completion rate with low CPU use on the workers
A growing backlog whose wait time keeps climbing
A latency budget that is comfortably under target
questions.explanation: Scaling is driven by backlog: growing queue depth and rising wait time mean workers cannot pick work up fast enough. An empty queue with idle workers is the signal to scale down, not up.

questions.question: Which pair of hard caps keeps a scaling worker pool from spending without limit?
options: A maximum pool size and a task-level rate limit
A minimum replica count and a fixed batch size
A maximum thread count and an unlimited daily budget
A fixed memory request and a disabled quota
questions.explanation: A pool that scales up forever can overshoot the provider's quota or the budget, so you cap the number of workers and rate-limit executions against the model endpoint. Both are security and cost controls, not just billing hygiene.

questions.question: Why does scaling agent workers on CPU lag behind a queue-driven workload?
options: CPU metrics are unavailable unless a device plugin is installed
CPU rises only after work is already being processed
CPU-based scaling is disabled whenever a pod requests a GPU
The autoscaler only ever scales down on CPU, never up
questions.explanation: CPU is a lagging reflection of work already in flight. A burst of queued tasks does not raise CPU until workers process them, and an agent waiting on a model call sits idle in CPU terms while tasks wait.

questions.question: How does event-driven autoscaling relate to the built-in pod autoscaler?
options: It extends the built-in autoscaler with external queue metrics
It replaces the built-in autoscaler, which must then be removed
It sets node taints so agent pods land on GPU nodes
It scales only on CPU and memory and never reads event sources
questions.explanation: Event-driven autoscaling works alongside the built-in autoscaler rather than replacing it. It feeds external metrics such as queue depth, and its operator handles scaling between zero and one replica of an idle workload.

questions.question: How does a pod request a GPU exposed as an extended resource?
options: In the requests field, so the GPU can be shared and overcommitted
In a separate plugin spec that bypasses the resource block
In the limits field, because the limit satisfies the request
In both fields, with requests set larger than limits
questions.explanation: For an extended resource the limit is what Kubernetes uses to satisfy the request, so a GPU is declared in the limits field. These resources are integer-only and cannot be overcommitted or shared between containers.
